title: The Back Office: ERP Integration and Who Is the Hub
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/23-erp-and-back-office-integration/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a thesis paragraph p04, a roadmap p06, a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening p52, and Part V's closing p57-p58); see decision_log.

know: The ERP's four jobs in a commerce business (the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation, master data) and the boundary between stock quantity, owned by the WMS, and stock value, owned by the ERP under IAS 2 and a costing method.
The flows between the commerce systems and the ERP (orders, shipments, payments and refunds, invoices, products, stock, customers and terms) with the system of record, direction and cadence of each.
The four hub answers (the ERP, the commerce platform, an OMS, an iPaaS with no hub) with where each fits and breaks, and the master-data ownership table for an Omnichannel merchant.
believe: Finance can be batch; availability cannot: the ERP is the system of record for finance and never the system a storefront waits on.
'Who is the hub' is a scale-stage decision, and an iPaaS with no hub is an accident, not a design.
The connector an ERP partner builds is a contract the merchant must own, written field by field before it is replaced.
can_do: Spot an ERP in a real-time path (availability, order status, checkout) and say what should replace it there.
Read a vendor connector's documentation as an entity–owner table, and write a field-level contract for an ERP connector: direction, cadence, system of record and the rule when the two disagree.
Choose the integration hub for a given business shape and stage.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an omnichannel merchant whose stock and prices pass through the ERP and its partner's undocumented connector, the reader says what is wrong and what the ERP should own and receive, not a bigger ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand with its own warehouse, six stores, a wholesale portal and three marketplaces sends stock from its warehouse system to its ERP every 15 minutes and from the ERP to the storefront hourly; its ERP partner's connector also copies orders hourly and pushes a price list, and nobody inside the company can say which fields it moves. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, and what should the ERP own and receive?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The ERP sits in the path of the sale: its cycle adds to the storefront's stock latency (an oversell), and a silent failure in its connector reaches customers (a wrong price for days). At this stage the ERP owns finance only (ledger, invoices, receivables, purchasing, stock value, item cost, business customers' prices, terms and credit, which leave it as events) and receives orders, shipments and payments by daily batch from the systems that own them; physical stock comes from the WMS and availability from an OMS or availability service by events. The connector gets a written field-level contract with direction, cadence, system of record and a rule for disagreement, a named owner, idempotent handling and a reconciliation job, and is then retired flow by flow.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three business shapes, the reader names the integration hub for each and what is wrong with having none.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which system should be the integration hub for a direct-to-consumer brand with one storefront and one warehouse, for a B2B-heavy business with one channel and one warehouse, and for a merchant with stores, wholesale and marketplaces in several countries? What is wrong with having no hub?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The commerce platform for the direct-to-consumer brand, with the ERP subscribing for finance; the ERP (or an ERP-driven store) for the B2B-heavy business with one channel and one warehouse; an OMS for the omnichannel merchant, with the ERP finance-only. An iPaaS with no hub is not a design but what happens when systems are connected as they arrive: point-to-point flows and nobody owning the cross-channel order record (Kestrel & Pine's thirty-four integrations and three definitions of 'order'); acceptable only as a transition.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what prevents duplicate sales orders in the ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: a platform webhook fires twice and the nightly order batch to the ERP is re-run after a partial failure. What goes wrong, and what prevents and detects it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The ERP holds two sales orders and double revenue for one order. The batch enforces one ERP document per order number (idempotent handling), reports per line rather than per file, and a daily count of orders in the OMS against sales orders in the ERP detects a difference; after posting, a reversing entry referencing the original.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: What the ERP keeps in a commerce business (the ledger, purchasing, stock valuation, master records); how it becomes the hub by accident and why the storefront's need for fresh stock cannot wait for the accounting cycle; which facts the ERP owns, which it consumes and how often each must move; the ERP compared with a commerce platform or an OMS as the hub; Eva's €235 order, payment, fee, shipment and any refund becoming postings for Sanne de Wit's April close. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's ERP connector and incidents, and ERP and connector vendors' documentation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].
The reader can say which system knows how much stock there is and which knows what it is worth, and why a storefront must not take availability from the ERP.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which system knows how many jackets are on the shelf, which knows what they are worth, and why should a storefront not read availability from the ERP?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The WMS knows the quantity; the ERP knows the value (inventory valuation under IAS 2 and a costing method). The ERP works on batch cycles and changes slowly in audited releases, so availability routed through it is late (the Black Friday Oversell); availability comes from the WMS and an OMS or availability service by events.

thesis.question: What does the ERP do in a commerce business, what should it own, and should it be the hub of integration?
thesis.claim: The ERP keeps the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and the master data for items, costs and business customers' prices, terms and credit; it should own only those facts and receive orders, shipments and payments by batch from their owners. It can be the hub while one channel sells from one warehouse; once several channels create orders needing availability in seconds, an OMS is the hub and no sale waits on the ERP.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the ERP is the natural hub because it already holds items, stock, prices, customers and orders: every system should connect through it, channels should read stock and prices from it, and the connector its implementation partner built is part of the ERP relationship rather than a contract the merchant owns.
thesis.so_what: At Kestrel & Pine the ERP sat in the stock chain between the WMS and the platform, adding up to an hour to the delay behind the Black Friday Oversell; its partner-built connector, undocumented and not idempotent, carried the German price-list push that failed silently in the Price Drift and invoiced only on the WMS 'order complete' message that left #1052877 'Not invoiced' for six days; and January 2027's close took eleven working days because marketplace orders arrived as a weekly summary and store sales as a nightly total. Waypoint's finance-only rule takes the ERP out of every real-time path and retires the connector flow by flow after Ruben Alves writes its field-level contract. A merchant that accepts the claim names a system of record per flow with a rule for disagreement, and writes its ERP connector's contract before replacing it.
thesis.how_why: A ledger needs every order, shipment, payment and refund once and complete, not within the minute, and a finance system changes in careful releases under audit, so a daily batch suits it. Availability and order status change by the minute and with the storefront's frequent releases, so a stock figure or status routed through the ERP's cycle arrives late and changes at the ERP's pace. With one channel and one warehouse there are no separate order and stock systems to integrate, so an ERP-centered store is the cheapest design; when stores, wholesale and marketplaces each create orders, they need one cross-channel order record and an availability calculation that an ERP's batch cycle cannot serve. A connector only its builder can read cannot be checked, changed or replaced, so its field-level contract is what the merchant must own.

supporting_claims.claim: The ERP's jobs in a commerce business are the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and master data for items, costs and business customers' prices, terms and credit; stock quantity belongs to the WMS and stock value to the ERP, and nothing in the path of a sale belongs in it.

Orders, shipments, payments and refunds reach the ERP by daily batch from the systems that own them, what the ERP owns for channels leaves it as events, and availability never comes from it, because finance needs completeness while availability needs seconds and the ERP changes in slow, audited releases.

Who is the hub depends on the business shape and scale stage: the ERP for one channel and one warehouse, the commerce platform for a D2C brand with one or two channels, an OMS at the Omnichannel and Group stages; an iPaaS with no hub is an accident.

Ownership of each master record and each flow is decided per entity and per field, with a rule for disagreement; a vendor connector encodes such a table, and its rules fit only the merchant it was built for.

The connector an ERP partner builds is a dependency the merchant must turn into a contract it owns (field-level specification, named owner, idempotent handling, reconciliation, failure alert) before replacing it flow by flow.

role.contribution: Places the ERP behind every channel: the system of record for finance that receives by batch and publishes what it owns for channels as events, the hub decision by scale stage, and the partner's connector as a contract the merchant owns; performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with Questions to Ask and a one-paragraph hand-off to Part VI).

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene: the connector nobody could read and the incidents it caused, then Waypoint's finance-only rule
hub, trade-offs and stages: the hub answers, then compared on the same criteria, then by scale stage

flow.rationale: The scene comes first so that every term arrives as part of the answer to Sanne's question of what the ERP should be the truth for. The ERP's four jobs come next because the flows section uses them (what each job needs from commerce). Batch and events follow the flows because they name the cadences the flows table assigns and give the rule (finance can be batch, availability cannot) that the hub question then rests on. The hub answers follow, and the trade-offs and stages come at once after them, because they turn the answers into a rule for choosing and place it on the book's stages. Connectors follow the stages because the first two stages rest on connectors, and a connector is where each flow's direction, cadence and owner are configured; master data follows connectors because the connectors raise, entity by entity, the question the ownership table settles. What never belongs in the ERP comes after the table that settles its grey area, and the partner dependency with it; the worked cases then apply the rule and the owned contract, and the failures come last because each is read against the design that detects it. Putting the hub before the flows and their cadences would argue a hub without the requirements that decide it (readers in round 1 found batch and events, placed after the stages, came too late for terms the flows and hub already used); separating the trade-offs and stages from the hub leaves the answers without a rule for choosing; putting master data before connectors presents the ownership table before the reader sees why a connector forces the choice; putting the cases before the partner remedy (the round-1 order) applied the remedy before stating it; putting the failures earlier would describe detections for a design not yet explained.

hook.content: When finance closes the books it must connect sales, payments, fees and refunds; the ERP that keeps that ledger holds so much data that other systems connect through it, and its scheduled updates end up deciding how quickly a shopper learns that a jacket has sold out.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has worked near a month-end close knows finance's question: what did the business earn and what is it owed, and from which records.
bridge.to_topic: The system that answers it, the ERP, is also the one every other system is tempted to connect through, so the question becomes what the ERP should own, what it should only receive and how often, and whether it should be the hub.

thesis_statement.text: The ERP should own the books, not the shop: the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and the master records for items, costs and business customers' prices, terms and credit, receiving orders, shipments and payments in daily batches from the systems that own them. It can be the hub while one channel sells from one warehouse; once several channels create orders and need availability in seconds, an OMS is the hub and no sale waits on the ERP.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and paragraph p04

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: The Connector Nobody Could Read
sections.controlling_idea: At Kestrel & Pine an ERP that held too much, joined to the shop platform by a partner-built connector nobody inside could read, sat behind three incidents and an eleven-day close, and Waypoint narrows it to finance.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the cost of an ERP in the path of the sale and of a connector the merchant does not own, and states Waypoint's answer the chapter generalises.

flow.rationale: The ERP and its connector first, then what Noor found, then the incidents and the close it caused, then Waypoint's answer; the answer cannot come before the reader has seen what it fixes, and the incidents only make sense once the connector's behaviour is known.

transition_in.carries_over: The roadmap's first item: the connector nobody could read.
transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's ERP, its partner and the connector between them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine has run a cloud ERP since 2023 for finance, purchasing, valuation, item records and invoices, wholesale staff key 38% of wholesale orders into it, and its connector to the shop platform was built by an outside implementation firm, the ERP partner.

evidence.what: Cloud ERP since 2023; 38% of wholesale orders keyed by hand; the partner-built connector.
evidence.shows: Shows how much the ERP holds and who built its main integration.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When Noor Visser asked the partner in January 2027 which fields the connector moves, how often and which system wins, she received a configuration export and a bill, and she and Ruben Alves needed three weeks to reconstruct its behaviour.

evidence.what: A configuration export, a bill and three weeks of reconstruction.
evidence.shows: The merchant did not know what its own integration did.

transition_in.carries_over: The partner-built connector.
transition_in.introduces: How opaque it was to its owner.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The reconstruction showed a connector that copies orders hourly, invoices only on the WMS's 'order complete' message, relays stock and German consumer prices on a schedule, is not idempotent and leaves failed runs until the next day.

evidence.what: Hourly order copy, invoicing on 'order complete', scheduled stock hops, the DE price list, no idempotency.
evidence.shows: Each behaviour is a way the ERP sat in a real-time path or failed silently.

transition_in.carries_over: The three weeks of reconstruction.
transition_in.introduces: What they found.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three of 2026's incidents ran through this connector: the Black Friday Oversell, because the ERP sat in the stock chain; the Three-Status Order, because invoicing waited for 'order complete'; and the Price Drift, a price push that failed silently for nine days.

evidence.what: The Black Friday Oversell, the Three-Status Order #1052877 (six days 'Not invoiced'), the Price Drift (nine days).
evidence.shows: Each incident traces to one of the connector's behaviours.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a stock figure relayed from the WMS through the ERP and a connector to the storefront, with the delays.

evidence.shows: Finance suffers from flows that arrive late and in different shapes.

sections.heading: What an ERP Does in a Commerce Business
sections.controlling_idea: An ERP has four jobs in a commerce business, the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and master data, and only it knows what the stock is worth.

advances_thesis.how: Names the jobs the ERP should keep and draws the quantity–value boundary.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ERP has four jobs a commerce architect should be able to name, the ledger, purchasing, inventory valuation and master data, and none of them needs anything from commerce in real time.

evidence.what: Four jobs with what each means, what it needs from commerce and what commerce needs from it.
evidence.shows: Shows that none of the jobs needs anything from commerce in real time.

sections.heading: Batch or Events: The ERP's Rhythm
sections.controlling_idea: Finance can work in daily batches while availability needs events, chiefly because a finance system changes slowly, and Kestrel & Pine's stock chain shows what breaks when the rule is ignored.

advances_thesis.how: Explains why the ERP's cadence suits finance and must not become the storefront's.

flow.rationale: The flows table's cadences named, then the rule, then its main reason (change, not performance), then Kestrel & Pine's breach as the example; both round-2 readers asked for the reason directly after the rule, where it supports it.

transition_in.carries_over: The cadence column of the flows table.
transition_in.introduces: What a batch and an event are and which rhythm each flow needs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The flows table gives each flow a cadence: a batch exchanges accumulated changes on a schedule and an event reports one change, and ERP connectors commonly run scheduled jobs whose cadence must be checked against each flow's required freshness.

evidence.what: Business Central: inventory sync every 15–30 minutes; OneStock: hourly or nightly; Shopify: real time or a daily batch (August 2026).
evidence.shows: Batch is the vendors' default, so the cadence is an operating choice per flow.
evidence.source: Microsoft Learn; OneStock; Shopify Enterprise blog, 2026

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Finance can often work in batches while availability needs fresher answers, so each fact's owner publishes changes and consumers process them at the cadence their work needs.

transition_in.carries_over: Cadence as an operating choice.
transition_in.introduces: The rule for choosing it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The business reason to keep the ERP out of the real-time path is change, not performance: a finance system changes carefully in audited releases while availability logic changes weekly, so coupling them lets the slow one set the pace.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule that finance can be batch while availability cannot.
transition_in.introduces: The deeper business reason for it: change, not performance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's 2026 stock chain, described in the scene, broke the rule that finance can be batch while availability cannot, and the Black Friday Oversell exposed the delay.

evidence.what: The 2026 stock chain and the Black Friday Oversell.
evidence.shows: A batch cadence in an availability path oversold.

evidence.what: Figure 4: availability as a live pulse in the path of the sale; the ERP receiving a daily batch behind a fence.
evidence.shows: Shows the two rhythms kept apart.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule and its reason.
transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's breach of it, pointing back to the scene.

sections.heading: Who Is the Hub? Three Answers and a Non-Answer
sections.controlling_idea: There are three honest answers to which system is the integration hub, the ERP, the commerce platform and an OMS, each right for a different business shape, and one accident, an iPaaS with no hub.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the hub options with where each fits and breaks, and places Waypoint's rule among them.

flow.rationale: Definition first, then the three answers from the smallest business shape to the largest, then the accident, then Kestrel & Pine's choice; the choice cannot be read before the options.

transition_in.carries_over: Finance can wait for batches; availability cannot.
transition_in.introduces: The question which system the others should connect through.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: If finance can wait for batches and availability cannot, the next question is which system the others connect through: an integration hub is the one system every other system connects through and that owns the shared records, and there are three honest answers and one accident.

With the ERP as hub every system integrates with the ERP, which holds stock, prices and customers; ERP-driven web stores such as Sana Commerce sell this, and it fits one channel, one warehouse, a B2B-heavy business and a small team because it avoids separate systems.

evidence.what: Sana Commerce: 'built on your SAP or Dynamics ERP', 'the prices you agreed and the stock you really have'.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With the commerce platform as hub the platform owns orders, customers and stock and the ERP subscribes for finance, as Business Central's Shopify connector describes; it fits a D2C brand with one or two channels and breaks when stores, wholesale and marketplaces bring their own order sources.

evidence.what: Business Central Shopify connector documentation, October 2026: orders flow into Business Central with the Shopify order id kept.
evidence.shows: A vendor documenting the platform-as-hub division.

evidence.what: OneStock (a vendor source): 'ERPs update inventory in batch cycles, hourly or nightly'; 'ERP isn't broken. It's just not built for everything.'
evidence.shows: The OMS argument, read as a vendor's case.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform as hub.
transition_in.introduces: The OMS as hub.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An iPaaS with no hub is not a design but what happens when each system is connected as it arrives: no system owns the cross-channel order record, which is how Kestrel & Pine came to thirty-four integrations and three definitions of 'order'.

evidence.what: 34 integrations; three definitions of 'order'.
evidence.shows: The cost of having no hub.

evidence.what: Hub table: what each means, fits, breaks when.

sections.heading: What Never Belongs in the ERP, and the Partner as a Dependency
sections.controlling_idea: Anything in the path of a sale never belongs in the ERP while postings and legal documents always do, and the partner's connector is a dependency the merchant must turn into a contract it owns.

transition_in.carries_over: The ownership table, which settles the grey area of master data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With the ownership table in place the rest of the boundary is plain: things in the path of a sale never belong in the ERP; postings, stock cost, legal invoices, receivables and purchasing always do.

Behind the line between the ERP and the commerce systems sits the ERP implementation partner, an unlisted architectural dependency, the Lynchpin, and the remedy is to treat the connector as a contract the merchant owns, with a field-level specification, an owner, idempotent handling, a reconciliation job and a failure alert.

evidence.what: Waypoint's W5 (integration standards) applied to one integration.
evidence.shows: The remedy is the program's integration standard, not firing the partner.

transition_in.introduces: The firm that built the link across that line, as a dependency.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Finance's question at the start, what the ERP should be the truth for and what it should just receive, has one answer across the sections: the ERP is the truth for the books and receives everything else by daily batch from the system that owns each fact, so the shopper learns that the jacket has sold out from the availability service, not from the accounting cycle; the hub follows the business shape, and the connector that carries the books is a contract the merchant writes and owns. For the part: the marketplace strike, the hand-keyed wholesale orders, Bergzicht's deduction and the eleven-day close are one problem, a value sent to an outside party from a copy or a system that did not own it, or an order kept in the tool its channel arrived through.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that keeps the ERP to finance gets a complete, reconciled ledger and a storefront that never waits on accounting; Kestrel & Pine's Part V remedies are ownership decisions and contracts more than new channels or platforms, so a reader can list, for each outside channel, where its orders are created, which system computes each value it is sent, and who owns its rules and dates.

callback.to: The introduction's ERP whose scheduled updates decide how quickly a shopper learns that a jacket has sold out, and Sanne's question; and, for the part, the part opening's jacket sold through a marketplace and a retail chain, where an extra sale handled like a consumer checkout ends in a penalty or a deduction.
callback.how: p52 answers the chapter's opening with the finance-only rule; p57 returns to the part opening and names the one problem behind its cases; p58 and p58a give the part's so-what and take-away.

takeaway.content: For each flow between commerce and the ERP, name the system of record and the rule when two systems disagree, and write the ERP connector's field-level contract before replacing it; for the part, list for each outside channel where its orders are created, which system computes each value it is sent, which rule or date the outside party enforces and who owns it, and whether any sale waits on the ERP.
